notes: Electricity split is well evidenced (BREF 45-90% refrigeration, DECC 50% for meat processing, and a 2025 UK Environment Agency permit application with full sub-metering). Thermal evidence: the same UK site burns all its fuel in a single hot-water boiler for sterilisation/cleaning. Pig scalding/singeing carries no default share (beef/sheep default) — reassign ~15-20% of gas to it at pig plants.

Electricity split reuses the processing-operations rows of the DOE crushed rock profile, which match this activity's scope directly. Diesel is assigned wholly to mobile plant by engineering logic. No source found separating depot site-services electricity.

MECS 2022 Table 5.2 includes a 4-digit NAICS 3364 aerospace row, used directly (better than the NAICS 336 aggregate); its transcription was noisy so values were reconstructed and validated against subtotals — treat cell values as approximate. A peer-reviewed study of 28 US aerospace facilities (AERO_FACILITY_2023) was checked and confirmed that no facility-level end-use disaggregation exists in the literature; UK OEM disclosures (Airbus/Rolls-Royce) publish totals only.

Electricity dominance of electrolysis is well evidenced (LBNL step intensities seen; IAI publishes the smelting AC intensity metric, whose definition — including rectification and auxiliaries, excluding casting and carbon plants — was verified on the IAI statistics page). No published per-vector site-level breakdown was found for the sole remaining GB smelter (ALVANCE Lochaber, hydro-supplied), so shares are engineering-tier derived from published per-step intensities. Anode production is marked optional since some smelters import baked anodes.

No published unit-operation energy split for man-made fibre plants was found. The Polymers BREF confirms scope and gives only whole-plant SECs (e.g. viscose staple 20-30 GJ/t direct energy, Table 13.13/Ch.11) without an operational breakdown, so all shares are engineering tier from rated-equipment logic. A wet-spinning (viscose/acrylic) alternative set was not supplied because no evidenced split exists; wet routes are far more steam-intensive (spin-bath evaporation, washing, drying).

The 2023 ENERGY STAR asphalt guide gives a published plant-level energy split (burner 80%, hot oil heater 12%, equipment 4%, electricity 4%; 317 MJ/ton), which fixes the fuel-vector profiles directly. The electricity sub-split is not published and is engineering-tier from motor ratings; evidence is US but the plant configuration matches UK practice.

Quantitative anchors come from the PBL/MIDDEN Dutch sugar study (steam 2.805 GJ and electricity 0.557 GJ per t sugar; pulp-dryer gas 6.10 GJ/t dry pulp; lime kiln cokes 3.4 GJ/t lime); the steam sub-split and electricity split are engineering allocations because the plant is heat-integrated and no published sub-split exists. British Sugar publishes intensity trends but no end-use split; UK sites run gas CHP, so metered gas covers both steam and pulp drying.

Full published electricity and thermal end-use splits from the Brewers Association energy manual (US, all brewery sizes); the 35% refrigeration figure is corroborated for UK breweries by the 2015 DECC roadmap report. UK-specific Carbon Trust CTG058 was not located online.

Process list is well evidenced (DECC Ceramic Report Sections 3.2.1-3.2.5; sector is 82% gas / 13% electricity per Section 3.3.3). No published percentage split of gas between kiln and dryer was located, so the thermal split is engineering-tier anchored to DECC Figure 10 and benchmark SEC ranges; electricity split is rated-equipment logic only. 2026-08-24: clay pit mobile plant added; metered oil attributed to it at engineering tier.

No published energy audit specific to concrete roof tile works was located; the process list is built from the well-documented precast/CMU analogues plus the tile-specific extrusion/pallet/coating loop, and all shares are fallback-tier borrowed from the LBNL-5342E precast (gas) and block (oil, electricity structure) profiles.

Strong published evidence: LBNL/ENERGY STAR gives a complete six-way electricity breakdown for dry-process plants, and both LBNL and the UK DECC roadmap confirm essentially all combustion fuel goes to kiln pyroprocessing. Missing: a UK-specific electricity split and a separate share for clinker cooling and site services (embedded in the LBNL categories). 2026-08-24: quarry mobile plant diesel brought into scope; oil vector re-split 0.8 mobile plant / 0.2 kiln at engineering tier.

Heterogeneous activity. UKCHEM2015 gives the sector vector mix (36% electricity in 2012, Fig 6) and names the end-use categories but publishes no unit-operation split; DOECHEM2015 confirms 60% of fuel goes via boilers/CHP and that machine drives dominate electricity, without percentages by unit operation. All shares are therefore engineering tier hung on those published statements.

The Iron and Steel BREF (2013, PDF located) defines the plant sections and the STET 2024 oven energy analysis confirms underfiring heat dominance (51.2% of oven energy input used as coking heat), but no published electricity breakdown by section was found, so electricity shares are engineering-tier from rated-equipment logic. Underfiring at UK-style by-product plants normally uses internally returned coke oven gas rather than purchased gas, so metered-gas rows apply only where mains gas supplements underfiring.

LBNL-5342E covers CMU plants directly: curing takes 60% of plant energy, all natural gas goes to the curing kiln/boiler, diesel is forklift/loader fuel, electricity is 13% of total (Table 4, p.11). The electricity sub-split is engineering-tier; UK block plants using unheated/ambient curing would show a smaller gas meter but the same structure.

LBNL-5342E gives published precast data: curing is ~44% of plant energy, gas splits 85% boiler / 15% building heat (Table 5, p.12), electricity ~17% of total. The electricity sub-split and the fuel-oil-to-boiler attribution are engineering-tier. LPG use (42 kBtu/yd3 in Table 5) had no stated end use, so no 'other' vector rows are supplied.

LBNL-5342E provides a rare published end-use split for ready-mix plants covering electricity (mixer 65%, water pump 20%, dust extractor 3%), gas (boiler 76% / building heat 24%) and diesel (boiler 54% / trucks 40% / building heat 6%). US data (2011) but directly analogous to UK batching plants; heating is seasonal (frost protection).

Electricity split is published (LBNL/Energy Star Figure 4.3, US) and consistent with the UK 25% refrigeration figure for liquid milk; fuel is published only at the 80/20 process-vs-building level, so the process-heat sub-split is engineering allocation using Ramirez-derived product tables. Site product mix (powder vs liquid vs cheese) moves the evaporation_drying share strongly.

Strong UK published evidence that ~85-90% of malt distillery heat goes to distillation (Scottish Enterprise/Ricardo hydrogen study; Briggs of Burton); electricity end-use split is unpublished and built from case-study equipment lists. Grain distillery split is engineering judgement only — no published unit-operation breakdown was found.

Coal Authority annual reporting provides scheme counts, treated volumes and total electricity (30,482,157 kWh in 2023-24) and attributes demand to pumping, but no process-level percentages; shares are engineering-tier reflecting the largely passive nature of UK minewater treatment. Only the electricity vector is material.

No published data specific to fast-fit exhaust/tyre centres was found; the profile is a fallback copy of the vehicle repair garage split, which is operationally the closest sibling (same building type and equipment classes, with somewhat higher compressed-air duty).

Anchored on MECS 2022 Table 5.2 NAICS 333 (machinery) as the generic discrete-manufacturing proxy, corroborated qualitatively by Carbon Trust CTV059 (motors ~25% of site electricity, lighting >10%, space heating 11% of manufacturing energy). US sector-level proxy for a UK site class, so confidence capped at medium; oil/coal/biomass rows omitted (no end-use evidence; oil-fired sites would mirror the gas split).

Milling is an almost entirely electrical activity (~75% of electricity in motors; 4-7 kWh/cwt US benchmark). The only unit-operation percentage found published is the pneumatic/high-pressure fan share (23-28%, Bühler); the remainder is engineering allocation. UK Flour Millers/nabim publish no public end-use split.

No single published unit-operation split exists for a generic food factory; profile is built from the technology shares (boilers 54%, direct heating 27%, motors 12%, refrigeration 5%, compressed air 2%) and the subsector refrigeration table in the 2015 DECC/BIS Food and Drink roadmap report.

Strong published evidence: DOE/Eppich 2003 facility audits give per-facility electricity and gas breakdowns by unit operation (multiple exhibits seen), and DOE Advanced Melting Technologies confirms melting at ~55% of total foundry energy. Values are US (2003) so confidence is medium; central values were synthesised across the audited cupola, induction and arc facilities to represent a generic UK foundry. No UK-specific (BCIRA/CMF) quantitative audit was located online.

Lime is used as the archetype for this NEC group, with strong EuLA/Ecofys evidence: kiln heat is 'by far the majority' of energy, electricity ~60 kWh/t (~5% of total) with BREF per-function kWh/t ranges enabling an engineering electricity split. Plaster/gypsum works (low-temperature kettle calcination ~150-165 degC) and calcined clay plants differ in kiln type and temperature but share the same crush-calcine-mill-pack structure; no separate published split was found for them.

Not-elsewhere-classified catch-all: profile is a fallback copy of the generic 'Factory' (MECS NAICS 333) split. The UK BEES survey publishes a Factories-sector end-use split that would be a better UK anchor, but its sector reports are only distributed in a ZIP that could not be retrieved in this session.

EAF set is the default: Port Talbot's blast furnaces closed in late 2024 and its EAF is under construction (construction under way in 2025-26, with CRU reporting possible delay to 2028), so Scunthorpe is GB's only remaining operating BF-BOF works, kept running under government direction since April 2025 (Commons Library CBP-10278); most operating GB steelworks (Celsa, Forgemasters, Liberty, and Port Talbot once commissioned) are EAF-based. No single published UK per-vector unit-operation breakdown was found — the DECC 2015 roadmap gives sector fuel mix (Figure 8) and CO2 by stage (Figure 7) but not energy-by-process — so shares are engineering-tier built on Stubbles/DOE process intensities. Internally generated works gases (COG/BFG, >60% of an integrated plant's energy per worldsteel) are excluded because they are not metered purchased vectors. Internal mobile plant diesel (scrap handling, slag transport) is in scope per the 2026-08-24 decision but no oil-vector split is populated yet - left absent (not assessed).

Strong UK evidence: the S-Lab/HEEPI audits of five UK university laboratories (Hopkinson et al. 2011) publish total-energy end-use splits (ventilation 45-60%, heating 20%, equipment 15-25%, lighting 5-10%; Table 7 p16); LBNL Labs21 material corroborates ventilation dominance. Shares here are the published split re-expressed per vector (heating assigned to gas, the rest to electricity), hence engineering tier despite the published basis. HVAC/ventilation is the dominant electricity process as required.

By definition (not elsewhere classified) no activity-specific evidence exists; the profile is a fallback copy of the generic 'Factory' (MECS NAICS 333) split, directionally supported by BEIS Business Energy Statistical Summary charts. Large NEC sites are heterogeneous — treat with low confidence.

Same evidence base as traditional maltings: kilning dominance is well attested (800 kWh/t kilning heat) but no published percentage split by unit operation was retrievable (CTG053 located on Issuu but unreadable); electricity shares are engineering estimates reflecting the additional germination-vessel fan load of pneumatic plants.

Kilning's dominance of malting fuel use is well supported (800 kWh/t kilning heat, Springer 2016; MAGB describes kiln heat recovery and fan VSDs as the principal measures), but no published unit-operation percentage split was located — Carbon Trust CTG053 exists (seen on Issuu) but its text could not be retrieved, so shares are engineering estimates.

No published end-use data specific to generic UK 'Mill' premises was found; the profile is a fallback copy of the 'Works' (MECS NAICS 332) split with plating reassigned to machine drive. The gas split assumes gas-fired drying exists; where a mill has no drying, expect space heating to dominate gas instead.

The Salt Association documents the full UK vacuum-salt process chain (solution mining, purification, multiple-effect evaporation, centrifuging, fluid-bed drying) but publishes no energy percentages, and the LVIC-S BREF was located but its salt energy tables were not verified; all shares are engineering-tier. Steam-raising for evaporation is unambiguously the dominant fuel use; sites with mechanical vapour recompression would shift evaporation load onto the electricity vector.

The DOE bandwidth study gives a genuine unit-operation breakdown for coal mining (Exhibit 20, p.27); the engineering step is allocating its categories to the electricity vs oil vectors (supported by the study's own diesel/electric splits, Section 3.2). US-average and 2007-vintage; remaining UK coal activity is surface-only, so ventilation and grinding shares overstate a UK surface site.

NSTA EMR 2024 verifies that power generation/compression combustion dominates UK upstream energy use (79% of offshore emissions; terminals 17% of industry total) but publishes no terminal-level unit-operation split, so the gas-vector shares are engineering-tier. Electricity-vector rows are omitted: no defensible split between electric compression, pumps and utilities was found.

A 2026 LCA of recycled-aggregate production supplies a real on-site diesel breakdown (loaders vs internal haulage) but only a facility-wide electricity total, so the electricity split is borrowed from the aggregates sibling. Sites running diesel mobile crushers will have materially different oil-vector shares; no published split for that configuration was found.

No published unit-operation energy breakdown for UK onshore oil production was located; NSTA emissions data are offshore-dominated (power generation 79% of 2023 offshore emissions, EMR 2024 Fig.3 p.8) and not process-resolved. Electricity shares are therefore engineering-tier rated-equipment logic; gas and oil vectors are omitted rather than guessed.

Catch-all category with no category-specific published split; the full profile is borrowed from the 'Rock, Sand, Clay' sibling, with the process list cross-checked against the DOE bandwidth industrial-minerals unit operations (Exhibit 22). Thermally-intensive 'other' minerals (e.g. with drying/calcining) are not represented.

Published totals are solid: AD parasitic electricity 59.1 kWh/t input (8.4% of gross output) and pasteurisation/digester heat 113.4 kWh/t at the UK Biocycle plant (IEA Bioenergy, Table 5); windrow composting 29 kWh/ton at 71% fuel / 29% electricity (van Haaren). Neither source sub-divides by unit operation, so all sub-splits are engineering-tier. Digester heat is normally self-supplied from biogas CHP, so no metered gas/biomass rows are given.

carb3_activity: Mineral Production - Rock, Sand, Clay etc.
notes: Best-evidenced activity. Published unit-operation splits from the US DOE limestone/crushed rock profile (2002) cover both the diesel (mining) and electricity (processing) vectors; NSSGA and MPA confirm mobile-plant diesel dominance in modern practice. Washing-plant and site-services electricity is not separated in any located source, so the electricity split covers the crushing-screening-conveying circuit only.

Strongest-evidenced activity in this group: electricity split comes from LBNL-50939 Table 2 (p.7), independently corroborated by ENERGY STAR Industry Insights 2015; gas split uses MECS 2022 NAICS 336 sector end uses interpreted via the LBNL narrative (paint ovens, steam/hot water, space heating). Both sources are US; no equivalent UK plant-level disclosure was found.

No published coldset-newspaper-specific energy split was found (Carbon Trust printing guide CTV028 could not be located). The PrintCity Alliance web offset report gives a plant-level production breakdown (drives 25-40%, process heating/cooling 30-50%, compressed air 5%, lighting <10%) which was adapted to coldset by removing the gas-fired dryer; all rows are therefore engineering tier.

Vector mapping per rule 7: internally generated fuels (refinery still gas and FCC catalyst coke) are metered as the 'other' vector and carry the published unit-level split (ENERGY STAR guide Table 3 p23, US 2011 data — the best per-unit breakdown found; UK Solomon/Concawe unit-level splits are not public); purchased natural gas ('gas') is allocated by engineering judgement to hydrogen production, boilers/cogen and supplemental heater firing; electricity is an engineering pro-rata allocation. Oil/coal vectors omitted (not material at UK refineries).

UK roadmap (s3.2.1) confirms GB stock is overwhelmingly recycled-fibre with only minority virgin (mechanical) pulping and no integrated kraft, so no kraft_integrated set is offered (no defensible UK split found). Published evidence gives the shape (paper machine ~2/3 of energy, dryer-dominated; stock prep/vacuum/drives dominate electricity) but not exact per-vector percentages, so shares are engineering-tier interpolations of UKPP2015 and LBNLPP2009 statements.

No published end-use split for mail sorting centres was found (Royal Mail reports disclose totals and initiatives, not end uses; the UK BEES Storage-sector split sits in an unretrievable ZIP). Profile is engineering-tier, anchored on Carbon Trust CTV073 warehousing evidence (lighting 65-95% of ambient warehouse energy, forklifts 7-10%) adjusted for the automated sortation load documented qualitatively for Royal Mail mail centres.

Process list is solidly evidenced (DECC Ceramic Report; whitewares have multiple firings and batch kilns). Quantified anchors are partial: firing ~87% of factory energy (MDPI tableware LCA) and drying ~9% of thermal energy (Qualicer tile study, analogue), so all shares are engineering-tier; the biscuit/glost split is assumed and flagged with wide ranges.

A published electricity split by equipment exists (trade press: pelleting 40%, milling 26%, mixing 9%, handling 6%, other 19%) and the steam/gas dominance of pellet conditioning (80-90%) is published; both are non-UK trade sources rather than peer-reviewed audits. No AIC UK-specific end-use data was located.

Coal Authority reporting confirms these sites are essentially single-purpose electric pumping loads (30.5 GWh purchased electricity in 2023-24, rising with volumes of mine water pumped), but publishes no percentage split, so shares are engineering-tier. No other vectors are material.

No published unit-operation energy breakdown for scrap/breakers yards was located; the BMRA article on shredding efficiency (located, fetched) confirms shredder electricity as the dominant controllable energy cost but gives no figures. All shares are engineering-tier from rated-equipment logic (multi-MW shredder motors vs diesel mobile plant); the shredding process is optional since most small yards only shear, bale and cut.

Best located evidence is the US EPA sector energy profile (fetched): electricity is 75-80% of shipyard energy expenditure and welding, forging/heating, abrasive blasting and coatings are the main energy-intensive processes, but no quantitative end-use split exists; a Bangladeshi shipyard case study (fetched) gives only vector-level intensities (96 kWh electricity and 12 kg LNG per tonne of steel), not end-use shares. All shares are therefore engineering-tier from rated-equipment logic anchored to the EPA process list.

The Tanning BREF and UNIDO framework confirm the structure (thermal energy to hot floats and drying; electricity to drums, machines, effluent treatment) and the MDPI Catalonian assessment gives the vector mix (gas 72-75%, electricity 25-27%), but no source located publishes a full per-operation split, so all shares are engineering tier; the Kano (Nigeria) audit anchors the machinery and lighting shares.

A real published end-use split exists (MidAmerican Energy auto-shop pie charts: electricity 33% shop equipment / 29% lighting / 12% ventilation etc.; gas 99% space heating). US utility data applied to UK garages, so medium confidence; no UK-specific (Carbon Trust) garage breakdown was found.

The Taiwan fab survey (Hu & Chuah 2003) publishes the top-level electricity split (facility systems ~56.6%, process tools ~40.4%) and enumerates facility subsystems; the subsystem split and the gas split are engineering allocations consistent with SST2004's 'HVAC up to 50% of fab electricity'. Statista/EPRI end-use breakdowns exist but were paywalled and not used.

Anchored on MECS 2022 Table 5.2 NAICS 332 (fabricated metal products), the best published match for a generic fabrication works; electricity and gas rows cross-checked against subtotals. Sector-level US data applied to a UK site class (medium confidence); other vectors omitted for lack of evidence.

No published workshop-specific end-use split found; electricity profile is a fallback copy of the 'Factory' (MECS NAICS 333) split and the gas profile is an engineering estimate anchored between CTV059 sector statements and garage evidence. Oil/coal/biomass omitted for lack of evidence (oil-heated workshops would mirror the gas split).
